description: Northern Ireland, the European question, nationalism in Scotland and Wales, and the Winter of Discontent.
content_html:
Civil Unrest in Northern Ireland

Northern Ireland entered a period of intense violence in the late 1960s and 1970s that became known as the Troubles. The conflict had deep roots in the partition of Ireland in 1921 and persistent discrimination against the Catholic and nationalist minority in the Northern Irish state. In 1968, inspired by civil rights movements elsewhere, Catholics began campaigning against discrimination in housing and voting. Clashes between protesters and police, and attacks by loyalist mobs, escalated rapidly.

British troops were deployed to Northern Ireland in August 1969, initially welcomed by some Catholics as protectors. The situation deteriorated rapidly. On 30 January 1972 — Bloody Sunday — British paratroopers shot dead 13 civilians taking part in a civil rights march in Derry (with a 14th dying later from wounds). The Saville Inquiry, reporting in 2010, found the killings unjustified and unjustifiable. The killings were a turning point: the Provisional IRA’s membership and support surged, and the violence intensified through the 1970s.

In March 1972, the British government suspended the Northern Ireland Parliament (Stormont) and introduced direct rule from Westminster — a measure intended as temporary that lasted, with brief interruptions, until 1998. The 1974 Sunningdale Agreement attempted a power-sharing executive between unionists and nationalists but collapsed after a loyalist workers’ strike within weeks. The conflict ground on, with bombing campaigns reaching the British mainland including Birmingham (1974) and the assassination of Lord Mountbatten (1979).

Key Fact

On Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972) British paratroopers killed 13 civilians at a civil rights march in Derry; a 14th died later. The 2010 Saville Inquiry concluded the killings were unjustified and unjustifiable. The event dramatically increased IRA recruitment and intensified the Troubles.

Sovereignty and Europe

Britain’s relationship with European integration was contentious throughout the 1970s. Harold Wilson’s Labour government had joined the European Economic Community (EEC) on 1 January 1973 — though in fact it was Edward Heath’s Conservative government that negotiated entry after two previous applications were vetoed by French President de Gaulle in 1963 and 1967.

The question of membership divided both major parties. In 1975, Harold Wilson’s Labour government held a referendum on whether to remain in the EEC — the first UK-wide referendum in history. The result was 67 per cent in favour of remaining, on a turnout of 64 per cent. However, the referendum did not settle the argument: Labour’s left wing remained hostile, and a minority of Conservatives were also sceptical of pooling sovereignty with European partners. The European question was a fault-line that ran through British politics for the rest of the century.

Opposition to EEC membership came from both left and right for different reasons. On the left, critics argued that the Common Market was a capitalist club that prevented Britain pursuing socialist economic policies — for example, it restricted state subsidies to industry. On the right, concerns focused on sovereignty — the idea that Parliament was the supreme source of law in Britain, and that pooling decision-making with European partners undermined this. The EEC also required Britain to accept the free movement of European workers, which some saw as a threat to British workers’ jobs and wages. These arguments — sovereignty, economics and migration — would resurface at every subsequent European debate over the following five decades.

Nationalism in Scotland and Wales

The discovery of North Sea oil in the early 1970s transformed the debate about Scottish independence. The Scottish National Party (SNP) used the slogan “It’s Scotland’s Oil” to argue that an independent Scotland could be economically self-sufficient. In the October 1974 general election, the SNP won 11 seats and more than 30 per cent of the Scottish vote. Plaid Cymru, the Welsh nationalist party, also grew, though from a smaller base and with a stronger cultural-linguistic focus than the SNP’s economic nationalism.

Both nationalist movements pushed the Labour government to consider devolution — transferring legislative powers to elected assemblies in Edinburgh and Cardiff. In March 1979, referendums were held in both Scotland and Wales. Scotland voted 52 per cent in favour of devolution, but a controversial amendment to the Scotland Act required 40 per cent of the entire eligible electorate to approve it — a threshold not reached. Wales voted against devolution by a large margin. The devolution question was shelved, to return more forcefully in the 1990s under Tony Blair.

The Winter of Discontent

The Labour government of James Callaghan ran into serious difficulties in the winter of 1978–1979. Attempting to hold public sector pay increases to 5 per cent to combat inflation, it faced a wave of industrial action. The Winter of Discontent saw lorry drivers, refuse collectors, gravediggers and public sector workers walk out. Images of uncollected rubbish piling up in Leicester Square and reports of the dead left unburied damaged public faith in the unions and in Labour’s ability to manage the economy.

The political consequences were severe. Margaret Thatcher’s Conservatives campaigned on a poster showing a long dole queue with the slogan “Labour Isn’t Working.” In March 1979 the Callaghan government lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote — partly because the SNP withdrew support after the failed devolution referendum. In the May 1979 general election, Thatcher won a majority of 43 seats. The Winter of Discontent had made her victory possible and gave her a mandate for fundamental economic reform.

Key Fact

The Winter of Discontent (1978–79) began when the Callaghan government’s 5 per cent pay cap provoked strikes by lorry drivers, refuse collectors, gravediggers and public sector workers. The resulting chaos destroyed Labour’s reputation for managing industrial relations and contributed directly to Thatcher’s general election victory in May 1979.

On 28 March 1979, James Callaghan’s government became the first UK government in 55 years to lose a vote of no confidence. The vote was 311 to 310 — a margin of one. The SNP’s 11 MPs voted against the government in protest at the failure of Scottish devolution. Some historians have described the vote as a paradox: nationalist MPs who wanted Scottish self-determination helped bring down the government most likely to offer it, installing Thatcher, who would oppose devolution for the next 18 years. The episode illustrates how the “Stuttering Seventies” were a decade of multiple, overlapping political crises destabilising the post-war settlement.
exam_tip_html: When answering a 16-mark Period Essay question about the 1970s, resist the temptation to narrate events chronologically. Instead, build your answer around the question’s concept — for example, if asked ‘how far was Britain in crisis in the 1970s,’ address economic instability (Winter of Discontent, inflation), political fragility (minority government, vote of no confidence), constitutional strain (Northern Ireland direct rule, devolution failure) and compare their relative severity. Reach a substantiated judgement at the end — don’t just describe all the crises.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972) killed 13 civilians in Derry and dramatically escalated the Troubles; direct rule was imposed from Westminster in March 1972 and lasted until 1998 with brief interruptions.
  • The 1975 EEC referendum confirmed British membership 67% to 33%, but the European question remained divisive; the SNP’s growth in the 1970s and failed 1979 devolution referendums left Scotland and Wales’ constitutional future unresolved.
  • The Winter of Discontent (1978–79) — strikes by lorry drivers, refuse collectors and gravediggers — destroyed Labour’s credibility and delivered Thatcher’s 1979 election victory on a mandate for economic transformation.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Troubles in Northern Ireland in the 1970s.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972) saw British paratroopers kill 13 civilians at a civil rights march in Derry.
• In March 1972 the British government suspended the Northern Ireland Parliament and introduced direct rule from Westminster.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Winter of Discontent in 1978-79.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• The strikes were triggered by the Callaghan government’s attempt to hold public sector pay rises to 5 per cent to combat inflation.
• Industries including lorry drivers, refuse collectors, gravediggers and public sector workers walked out.
• The crisis damaged public faith in the trade unions and in Labour’s ability to manage industrial relations.
• The political consequence was Thatcher’s Conservative victory in the May 1979 election.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Winter of Discontent in 1978-79.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the cause (the Callaghan government’s 5 per cent pay cap at a time of high inflation, when workers’ real wages were falling) and develops the mechanism — trade unions rejected the cap as unacceptable given inflation eroding living standards; Labour depended on union support but could not meet their demands; industrial action cascaded across the public sector.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972) for the conflict in Northern Ireland.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (surge in IRA recruitment and support, or the suspension of Stormont and introduction of direct rule) and develops the chain — killings inflamed nationalist opinion, fuelled IRA recruitment, led to escalation of bombing campaigns, and forced the British government to take political control through direct rule, which itself became a grievance.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1975 EEC referendum for Britain's relationship with Europe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (Britain’s first national referendum, confirmed EEC membership by 67-33%, appeared to settle the question) AND over time (failed to resolve the underlying divisions — Labour left and Conservative right remained hostile, the European question returned more forcefully in later decades, foreshadowing the 2016 Brexit referendum). Weighs how conclusive the result actually was.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the referendum without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Northern Ireland was the most serious crisis facing British governments in the 1970s.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing Northern Ireland alongside the European question, nationalist movements in Scotland and Wales, economic crises (inflation, IMF bailout 1976), and the Winter of Discontent. Weighs the relative severity of crises with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for and against the interpretation. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

flashcard_questions.a: The killings were unjustified and unjustifiable.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Britain join the European Economic Community?
flashcard_questions.a: 1 January 1973, under Prime Minister Edward Heath.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the result of the 1975 EEC referendum?
flashcard_questions.a: 67 per cent voted to remain in the EEC.

flashcard_questions.q: What slogan did the SNP use in the 1970s to argue for Scottish independence?

flashcard_questions.a: The transfer of powers from the central UK Parliament to elected assemblies in Scotland and Wales.

flashcard_questions.q: What outcome did the 1979 Scottish devolution referendum produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A majority voted yes but the 40% threshold of the entire electorate was not met, so devolution failed.

flashcard_questions.q: Which industries were involved in the Winter of Discontent strikes?
flashcard_questions.a: Public sector unions walked out across a range of essential services, most visibly lorry drivers who blocked food supplies and refuse collectors whose uncollected rubbish piled up in city streets.

By how many votes did Callaghan's government lose the vote of no confidence in March 1979?
When was the Northern Ireland Parliament (Stormont) suspended and direct rule imposed?

glossary_terms.definition: The period of violent conflict in Northern Ireland, roughly 1968 to 1998, between republican and loyalist paramilitary groups and British security forces, resulting in over 3,500 deaths.
A day on which British paratroopers shot dead 13 civil rights marchers in Derry, Northern Ireland, on 30 January 1972, causing a major escalation of the Troubles.
The European Economic Community, founded by the Treaty of Rome in 1957 as a common market; Britain joined in January 1973 under Edward Heath.
The party that campaigns for Scottish independence; it won its first Westminster seat in 1967 and grew significantly in the 1970s as North Sea oil strengthened the economic case.
The transfer of powers from the central UK Parliament to elected assemblies in Scotland and Wales.

The period of widespread strikes in the winter of 1978-79, when public sector unions rejected the government's 5 per cent pay cap, leading to rubbish left uncollected and lorry drivers blocking food supplies.

items.title: BBC Teach — 1970s Britain
items.description: BBC Teach's curriculum history channel covers the Troubles, the EEC debate, devolution and the Winter of Discontent with short clips designed for GCSE study.

items.title: Mark Felton Productions — Cold War and Modern Britain
items.description: Mark Felton covers modern British political and military history, including the conflict in Northern Ireland and its context within Cold War-era security concerns.

items.title: Bloody Sunday (2002)
items.description: Paul Greengrass's docu-drama reconstruction of the events of 30 January 1972 in Derry, showing the civil rights march, the Parachute Regiment's actions and their immediate aftermath.

items.title: In the Name of the Father (1993)
items.description: Jim Sheridan's drama about the Guildford Four — wrongly convicted for IRA bombings — examines the Troubles' impact on mainland Britain and the miscarriage of justice that followed.
Jack O'Connell plays a British soldier left behind in Belfast in 1971, offering an immersive ground-level view of the early Troubles and the impossible position of British troops on the streets.

items.title: Britannica — Bloody Sunday (Northern Ireland, 1972)
items.description: Encyclopaedia article on the events of 30 January 1972, the Saville Inquiry's findings and the significance of the killings for the escalation of the Troubles.

items.title: Britannica — Edward Heath
items.description: Biography of the Conservative Prime Minister who took Britain into the EEC in 1973 and imposed direct rule on Northern Ireland in 1972 — central to understanding the 1970s political landscape.

items.title: Britannica — Margaret Thatcher
items.description: Biography of the Conservative leader whose 1979 general election victory was made possible by the Winter of Discontent — covering her political rise and the mandate she received.

items.title: Britannica — Bloody Sunday (Northern Ireland, 1972)
items.description: Detailed reference article covering the sequence of events, the paratroopers' actions, the immediate political fallout and the long path to the Saville Inquiry's conclusions.

items.title: Britannica — James Callaghan
items.description: Biography of the Labour Prime Minister whose 5 per cent pay cap triggered the Winter of Discontent and whose government fell by a single vote in March 1979.

items.title: Hunger (2008)
items.description: Steve McQueen's unflinching film dramatises the 1981 IRA hunger strikes at the Maze Prison — rooted directly in the unresolved Troubles that had escalated through the 1970s.
